title: The Twenty-Four Priestly Divisions
summary: David, with Zadok and Ahimelech, divides the descendants of Aaron into twenty-four divisions, sixteen from Eleazar's line and eight from Ithamar's. The order of service is set by casting lots, with a Levite scribe recording the names. The chapter then lists further heads of Levitical families, who also cast lots before the king.
story: After organizing the Levites in general (chapter 23), David turns to the priests, the descendants of Aaron who alone offered sacrifices. This chapter creates the rotation system by which the priests would take turns serving in the temple. It is one link in a long chain of organization running from chapter 23 to chapter 27, all of it preparing for Solomon's temple. Though it looks like an administrative list, the system it sets up lasted for centuries, and it shows up again at the start of the New Testament.
historical:
Aaron had four sons. Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the LORD (Leviticus 10:1-2) and had no sons, so the priesthood passed through Eleazar and Ithamar. In David's day Zadok represented Eleazar's line and Ahimelech son of Abiathar represented Ithamar's (verse 3). Later, Solomon removed Abiathar from the priesthood (1 Kings 2:26-27), and Zadok's line became dominant in the Jerusalem temple.

The twenty-four divisions are known from later sources. Nehemiah 12 lists priestly families after the exile, several with names from this chapter. The eighth division, Abijah (verse 10), is the division of Zechariah, father of John the Baptist, in Luke 1:5. The first division, Jehoiarib, is the family of Mattathias, the priest who began the Maccabean revolt in the second century BC (1 Maccabees 2:1, where the name appears as Joarib). Many scholars think the chapter reflects the system as it operated in the Chronicler's own day, attributed to David as its founder; others take it as a Davidic institution continued through later centuries.
cultural:
With twenty-four divisions, each division served a week at a time in rotation, which later Jewish sources describe, plus all divisions serving together at the great pilgrimage festivals. Luke 1:8-9 reflects this system: Zechariah's division was on duty, and he was chosen by lot to offer incense. Casting lots was a common way of making decisions in Israel, understood as leaving the choice to God (Proverbs 16:33). It prevented rivalry between the more numerous line of Eleazar and the smaller line of Ithamar and removed human favoritism.

The recording of names by a Levite scribe in the presence of the king, the priests, and family heads (verse 6) made the arrangement official and public. Written records of priestly descent mattered deeply later: after the exile some families were excluded from the priesthood because they could not find their genealogical records (Ezra 2:61-62).
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-19 give the priestly divisions: background (verses 1-6), the list of twenty-four lots in a fixed formula (verses 7-18), and a summary grounding it in Aaron's command (verse 19). Verses 20-31 add a supplementary list of Levites that partly repeats and extends names from chapter 23, extending some families by a generation. The repetition of ordinals, first, second, third, up to twenty-fourth, gives the list a steady rhythm. The closing phrase of verse 31, the family heads and their younger brothers alike, stresses the fairness of the lot.

outline.t: Aaron's line divided between Eleazar and Ithamar
The twenty-four lots and their order of service
The remaining Levites also cast lots

doctrines.note: The lot was not seen as chance. Casting lots before the LORD placed the order of service in God's hands and kept human ambition out of it.

The priests served according to the regulations prescribed for them by their forefather Aaron (verse 19). The mention of Nadab and Abihu's deaths is a quiet reminder of what careless approach to the holy God cost.
The system shared the privilege and burden of service among all the priestly families, great and small. Order in worship here serves fairness and continuity across generations.

words.note: Goral, lot. Originally a small stone or marked object cast to decide a matter, it came to mean the portion assigned by lot, and so one's allotted share. The lot divided the land among the tribes under Joshua and now divides the service among the priests.
Machaloqet, division or course. It names the rotating groups of priests and Levites. Luke's reference to the division of Abijah (Luke 1:5) uses a Greek word for the same institution.
Avodah, service. The divisions were arranged according to the offices of their service (verse 3). The word covers both labor and worship, and in the temple they were the same thing.

christ: This dry list has a direct line to the Gospels. Luke opens his account with Zechariah, a priest of the division of Abijah, the eighth lot in this chapter, serving in the temple when an angel announces the birth of John the Baptist (Luke 1:5-13). The system David set up is still running when God begins the events that lead to Jesus. The New Testament also presents Christ as a high priest of a different kind: not one of many who rotate in and out, serving a week at a time, but one who serves forever and whose single offering is complete (Hebrews 7:23-27). The rotation of mortal priests underlines, by contrast, the permanence of his priesthood.
questions: The lot kept the more numerous family from dominating the smaller one. How can a community make sure that power and privilege are shared fairly?
Zechariah was serving in his ordinary, assigned turn when God met him. What might it mean to expect God in the ordinary rotation of your duties?
The priests served according to the regulations prescribed by Aaron. What role do inherited patterns and structures play in your faith, for good or ill?
